analysis.one_liner: Requires drug makers to sell to pharmacies at their lowest government price, cutting seniors' drug costs.
analysis.headline: The bill, which by its sponsors' estimate would have cut Medicare beneficiaries' drug prices by more than 40%, died in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have forced any drug maker that sells to the federal government to also sell to local pharmacies, in the quantities Medicare patients need, at the lower of two prices: the cheapest price any federal agency pays for the drug, or the manufacturer's 'best price' given to its biggest buyers. Pharmacies would then pass those prices on to Medicare beneficiaries, who today pay cash at retail rates. The bill's findings state that seniors on average pay twice as much as the government and other big buyers, sometimes more than 15 times as much, and estimate prices would fall by more than 40%. It also extended the pricing to drugs furnished through hospice programs and required annual reports on whether it worked.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who buy their own prescriptions, especially the roughly one in eight older Americans the bill says are forced to choose between food and medicine. Pharmacies buying at government-negotiated prices would also see lower acquisition costs, and taxpayers could save if Medicare pays for fewer high-priced drugs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare beneficiaries who pay cash for prescriptions

how_it_helps.text: Requires participating manufacturers to sell covered drugs to pharmacies at the lower of the lowest federal price or the manufacturer's best price, in quantities matching what pharmacies sell to Medicare beneficiaries.

The bill's findings state that seniors on average pay twice as much as manufacturers' most favored customers, sometimes over 15 times more, and estimate implementation would reduce drug prices for Medicare beneficiaries by more than 40%.
Extends the pricing benefit to drugs furnished to Medicare beneficiaries enrolled in Medicare-certified hospice programs, covering terminally ill patients.
Directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to report to Congress annually on whether the law actually reduced prices and to recommend further reductions.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, which would give up the wide gap between what big institutional buyers pay and what seniors pay at the pharmacy counter. The bill's own findings say the pricing practices sustain about $20 billion in annual industry profits. Any savings to taxpayers would be offset where manufacturers raise prices elsewhere or reduce output, a risk the bill does not address.

drawbacks.text: By pegging pharmacy prices to the lowest federal price or Medicaid 'best price,' the bill could push manufacturers to raise their base list prices to protect revenue elsewhere, the known distortion of the Medicaid best-price rule it borrows from.
The mandate applies only to manufacturers that contract with the federal government, so firms could avoid it, and the bill offers no alternative coverage for seniors beyond lower sticker prices.
The 40%-plus savings figure comes from the bill's own findings, not an independent estimate, and the bill provides no funding or analysis of how pharmacy supply arrangements would adjust.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit for seniors paying cash for prescriptions is large and direct, and the mechanism is simple: seniors get the same prices the government already gets. The main cost falls on drug makers, whose pricing practices the bill blames for $20 billion in annual profits. The design carries real risks of price-shifting through the best-price peg, and it was a single-sponsor bill with no hearing or analysis, so its assumptions were never tested. Still, on its face the benefits to seniors and taxpayers outweigh the costs to manufacturers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee in April 2003, and the committee never took it up; it died there when the 108th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Tim Johnson introduced the bill on April 11, 2003, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.
The Finance Committee took no further action; the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, and expired when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

Later that same year, Congress enacted the Medicare Modernization Act, which created a voluntary prescription drug benefit delivered through private insurers rather than direct price regulation; the direct-pricing approach in this bill was not part of it.

A nearly identical price-discrimination approach had passed the House in an earlier Congress but was never enacted, reflecting a long-running stalemate over direct government price leverage versus private drug coverage.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers were better off: the bill died without a hearing or cosponsor, and Medicare beneficiaries continued paying retail prices roughly twice what big institutional buyers pay. Congress instead created a drug benefit run through private insurers later that year.

for.name: Sen. Tim Johnson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Prescription Drug Equity for Seniors Act of 2003 and referred it to the Finance Committee.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after referral; it died in committee.

against.name: Sen. Charles Grassley
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never brought the bill before the committee in the two years it was pending.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had one Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, and no record of any vote; the pharmaceutical pricing fight of that Congress generally split along party lines, with the eventual Medicare drug benefit enacted by a Republican majority using private plans rather than direct price mandates.

industries.note: The bill would have ended their ability to charge seniors retail prices roughly double what the government pays, cutting into profits the bill's findings put at about $20 billion a year. Manufacturers avoided any loss because the bill died in committee.
Pharmacies would have bought drugs at government-level prices, lowering their acquisition costs while passing the savings to Medicare customers. Some margin on seniors' cash sales could shrink.

industries.industry: Private Medicare drug insurers and benefit managers
industries.note: When Congress created the Medicare drug benefit later that year, it routed coverage through private insurers and pharmacy benefit managers instead of direct price mandates like this bill's, making those intermediaries the permanent channel between seniors and drug prices.
